text: Mesoscale brain dynamics have been linked to a wide range of perceptual, cognitive and motor functions.
However, establishing causal links between mesoscale dynamics and behavior remains challenging, because it requires not only perturbing these dynamics but also precisely shaping them.

Here we show that closed-loop optogenetic inhibition can steer cortical activity in real time toward a target level, using feedback from the ongoing dynamics. We employed a system with simultaneous wide-field calcium imaging and laser-driven optogenetic stimulation at the cortical surface in mice.
In this preparation, the trial-averaged response of a cortical site when stimulated in open-loop is approximately linear and, within a session, time-invariant.
On this basis, we designed a closed-loop linear feedback controller with measured fluorescence as the input and laser intensity as the output.
The controller steered the activity to the target level more accurately than open-loop stimulation and reduced trial-to-trial variability.
Controller performance depended on brain state:

feedback removed more of the error that accompanied overt bodily movements of the mouse, despite the activity being less predictable whereas its error grew with spontaneous delta-band (1--4\,Hz) synchronized cortical activity.
Predicting the disturbance on each trial from the opposite hemisphere, we show that feedback partially rejects it.
For time-varying target levels, a preview component of the controller successfully compensated for system delays.

Finally, in a simulated replay of recorded trials with a constant reference, a model-predictive controller using a linear model of cortex and the laser lowers the error left by feedback by about 40\%.

Together, these results show that approximately linear, time-invariant trial-averaged dynamics can be used to control regional cortical activity, and that the error left under control is informative about brain state.
Significance Statement
We introduce a closed-loop control framework to steer cortical activity toward a target level.
Using wide-field calcium imaging, we read out activity at one cortical site in real time and used it to set optogenetic inhibition delivered next to it.
Closed-loop stimulation tracked the target level more accurately than open-loop, fixed stimulation and reduced trial-to-trial variability across sessions and animals.
The remaining error depended on cortical state during the stimulation, and a feedforward preview corrected phase lags when tracking time-varying targets.

Finally, a linear model based on measured activity of the opposite hemisphere predicted much of the spontaneous activity in the controlled region, allowing us estimate the disturbance the controller rejects on each trial.
Introduction
Precisely modulating the activity of a neuronal population can establish how it contributes to or affects behavior, which pathways mediate its influence, and how its effect depends on brain state.
Yet modulation, whether optical, electrical, or magnetic, is often delivered open loop, with an input pattern chosen in advance.

The response to any input depends on the circuit's current state, that is, its ongoing pattern of activity, as has been shown for sensory, optogenetic, and magnetic stimulation~\citep{Arieli1996, Petersen2003, Goris2014, Mateo2011, Massimini2005}.

In the cortex of awake mice, brain state is influenced by movements such as whisking or fidgeting and by arousal~\citep{Niell2010, McGinley2015, Vinck2015, musall2019single, stringer2019spontaneous, Salkoff2020}. State fluctuates between slow, synchronized rhythms during quiet wakefulness and desynchronized activity during engaged states ~\citep{Crochet2006, Poulet2008, Reimer2014}, and is shared across the two hemispheres~\citep{Mohajerani2010, Shimaoka2019, Ye2026}.
Momentary cortical activity is presumably driven by these well-characterized states along with unobservable states,  unmeasurable stimuli, and interactions from other brain regions.
Therefore, activity appears highly variable across trials of responses to a fixed stimulus.
One way to handle this variability is to adequately model it such that factors contributing to variability can be determined.
In literature several approaches have been explored, where the activity can be modeled through a dynamical systems.

Switching linear dynamical systems treat the state as a parameter that changes the dynamics~\citep{linderman2017rslds}, other models isolate the dynamics relevant to a behavior~\citep{sani2021modeling}, and cortical state can be estimated in real time~\citep{weiss2024realtime}.

Such models, however, do not observe the movements and the input from other areas that also drive a region~\citep{musall2019single, stringer2019spontaneous, zagha2013motor}, and even the best current models forecast spontaneous wide-field activity informatively only about 1.5\,s ahead~\citep{lu2025benchmarking} with considerable amount of uncertainty.

Machine-learning models of neural population dynamics have grown more capable, from sequential autoencoders~\citep{pandarinath2018lfads} and transformers~\citep{ye2021ndt} to learned latent embeddings~\citep{schneider2023cebra}, foundation models~\citep{wang2025foundation} and transformers that tokenize spikes and are pretrained across many recordings and animals~\citep{azabou2023poyo}.

For control, however, they have two limits: many infer activity from whole recorded trials~\citep{pandarinath2018lfads} or are computationally costly for real-time use, which recent hybrid state-space models address~\citep{ryoo2025possm}, and apart from models of responses to sensory stimuli~\citep{wang2025foundation}, they reconstruct or decode activity rather than forecast how it will respond to stimulation, as a controller needs.
A stimulus planned in advance would need a model that identifies and forecasts each trial's state precisely.

Closed-loop control, which adjusts the input continuously from a real-time measurement of the activity it is meant to control, can in principle correct for such differences, provided the activity can be read out fast enough and the input acts on that same activity.

Because it acts on each trial's measured deviation, feedback needs no model of what caused that deviation, so state-dependent activity that adds to the response becomes a disturbance to reject rather than a confound to average.
Mesoscale activity is the combined activity of local neural populations across millimeters of cortex, between the scale of single neurons and that of the whole brain.

Its spontaneous spatial patterns follow the axonal projections between regions~\citep{mohajerani2013spontaneous}, and it is closely tied to behavior, carrying task variables, learning-related change and movement~\citep{allen2017global, makino2017transformation, musall2019single}.
We read it out as fluorescence across a field about 10\,mm wide.

Wide-field imaging samples the field at 35\,Hz, and the latency, the delay from a camera exposure to the light it triggers, has a median of 24\,ms, about a fifth of the 0.11\,s timescale on which light moves the activity.

Spatially targeted optogenetic stimulation has been combined with wide-field imaging to map and silence cortical areas~\citep{Lim2012, ZatkaHaas2021, Matveev2024, Ambrosone2025}, but open loop: the stimulus is fixed in advance, and the variability it meets is averaged away afterwards.
In our setup, the light suppresses the cortex around the stimulated spot, including the region we read out.
Mesoscale activity is therefore a convenient scale at which to test closed-loop control, though not the only one.

Closed-loop stimulation has revealed what particular rhythms contribute to behavior: optogenetic stimulation triggered at chosen phases of hippocampal theta, or by bursts of amygdala gamma, showed their roles in encoding, retrieving and consolidating memories~\citep{Siegle2014, kanta2019closed}.
Closed-loop optogenetic feedback has also reshaped ongoing oscillations, in brain slices and in anesthetized monkeys~\citep{nicholson2018analogue, Zaaimi2022}.
Continuous control, which adjusts the input at every update instead of delivering a preset one, has held neuronal firing at a chosen level in culture and in vivo~\citep{newman2015optogenetic}.

Controllers designed from a model of the plant, the system the controller acts on, fitted to its responses to light, made thalamic firing track time-varying targets and reject unmeasured disturbances, and changed its trial-to-trial variability~\citep{bolus2018design, bolus2021state}.

For electrical stimulation, input--output models of multiregional responses have been built for model-based control~\citep{Yang2018, Yang2021} and tested in closed loop in simulation~\citep{Yang2018}.
All-optical loops have tailored two-photon stimulation to activity imaged in real time~\citep{Zhang2018, Zhang2025}.

Activity has also been fed back to animals as sound, from cortical neurons~\citep{clancy2014volitional, Neely2018} to mesoscale regions~\citep{Gupta2026}, but there the loop closes through the animal learning to change its activity for reward, not through a stimulus to the cortex.

Closed-loop stimulation of mesoscale activity thus remains largely unexplored: to our knowledge, a framework for closed-loop all-optical control of cortex-wide activity has so far appeared only in a conference abstract~\citep{deAlteriis2026}.
Three questions remain open.
First, is the response of a mesoscale signal to optogenetic input close enough to linear and time-invariant to design a controller from it?
Open-loop work shows that suppression of wide-field activity deepens with laser power~\citep{Ambrosone2025}, but a controller also needs the time course of the response.
A linear description is plausible, because linear models often predict brain activity about as well as nonlinear ones~\citep{Nozari2024}.

Control theory suggests it would also be enough, because low-gain integral control of a stable linear plant needs only the sign of its steady-state gain~\citep{logemann2000absolute}, which a monotonic response supplies.
Second, does feedback make the signal less variable from trial to trial than open-loop input?
Third, how does the error that feedback leaves depend on the circuit's state, which makes open-loop responses vary?
A controller designed on the average response is not designed for single-trial deviations, so relating the error it leaves to the measured state can show which fluctuations lie beyond its reach.
The answers decide whether closed-loop control can set mesoscale activity precisely enough to test what it contributes to behavior, and whether a controller should take the state into account.
Here we close the loop on mesoscale activity in awake, head-fixed mice.

A camera images calcium-dependent fluorescence across the dorsal cortex at 35\,Hz, and on every frame a controller compares the activity of a 0.17\,mm patch of somatosensory cortex with a reference level below baseline and sets the power of a laser aimed next to the patch.
The light excites inhibitory neurons that express an opsin, so it can only lower the activity.

We first characterized how the activity responds to pulses of light of different amplitudes and, on that basis, built a proportional--integral controller with feedforward compensation, tuned to the experiment, which we compared with open-loop stimulation within each session.

Trial-averaged suppression deepened with laser power, as in open-loop silencing~\citep{Ambrosone2025}, and was approximately linear and time-invariant within a session, so a low-order linear model predicted it, in four sessions from three mice.
Single responses, however, varied from trial to trial about as much as ongoing activity did without stimulation, and both changed together with the state.
Closed loop held the activity at the reference more accurately than open loop in all 15 sessions from four mice, and reduced its trial-to-trial variability.

Power at 1--4\,Hz, which marks large, slow fluctuations, raised the error of both by similar amounts, so feedback did not hold the activity at the reference as this power grew, whereas feedback removed more of the error that accompanied movement.

These results outline a procedure: characterize the input--output relationship, check that the average response is monotonic and approximately linear, and tune a proportional--integral controller to the experiment.

It assumes only a readout that is fast relative to the response and an input whose effect is close to linear, so it is not tied to wide-field imaging or optogenetics, although we test it here with one readout and one input.

The error that such a controller leaves then carries information about the state: it shows which components of ongoing variability lie beyond a fixed linear design, a starting point for controllers that take the state into account.
Results
We built a closed-loop optogenetic system that precisely regulates (i.e., steers) the activity of a cortical region, monitored with wide-field calcium imaging in mice.

The evoked responses to stimulation scaled monotonically with stimulus amplitude, and a linear time-invariant model captured their dynamics, which gave us an empirical basis for designing a controller.
We then show that this controller holds cortical activity at a target level and its regulation performance is informative about brain states.
Experimental setup and closed-loop control architecture
We performed closed-loop experiments in head-fixed transgenic mice co-expressing GCaMP and an inhibitory opsin.
Each mouse sat in a behavioral chamber facing a blank screen, with its forelimbs resting on a freely moving wheel, and was not engaged in any task, so all recordings captured spontaneous activity.

We recorded cortical activity at 35\,Hz with wide-field calcium imaging (Figure~\ref{fig:figure1}A) and delivered spatially targeted optogenetic stimulation to a fixed cortical spot, which suppressed activity in the surrounding cortex (\citep{Matveev2024} ; Figure~\ref{fig:spatial_spread}A,B).

We quantified cortical activity as the fractional change in fluorescence relative to its mean ($\Delta F/F$), averaged over pixels near the stimulation spot (Figure~\ref{fig:figure1}B,C; see Materials and Methods), and take this signal, which we call the 'output', as the quantity to be controlled.
In a subset of experiments, we also recorded video of the face and computed its motion energy as a behavioral co-variate.

We built an end-to-end software system for real-time closed-loop control  (Figure~\ref{fig:figure1}D).

At each imaging frame acquisition, the software collects the frame data, computes the error between the measured output and a reference $\Delta F/F$ value, and computes the required optogenetic stimulus amplitude. The system has a measured end-to-end loop delay of XX.X ms on average (mean; YY.Y-ZZ.Z range; Figure~\ref{fig:figure1}F).
This delay, together with the kinetics of the indicator and the opsin, limits the bandwidth over which feedback can act (see Discussion).
The controller combines a proportional--integral (PI) feedback term with open-loop (feedforward) compensation (Figure~\ref{fig:figure1}E).
The feedforward term supplies the nominal stimulus needed to reach the reference, scaled by a gain calibrated from open-loop stimulation experiments.

The PI term corrects the remaining error in real time as the brain state changes, compensating for an inaccurate feedforward gain, residual nonlinearities, and spontaneous trial-to-trial fluctuations.

The mean evoked suppression grew monotonically with stimulation amplitude: the stronger the stimulation, the deeper the trial-averaged suppression, even though single-trial responses varied (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}B; Materials and Methods).

This input--output relationship was approximately linear (slopes $-0.88$, $-1.32$, $-1.53$ and $-3.11\,\%\,\Delta F/F$ per mW; $R^2 = 0.97$, $0.73$, $0.88$ and $0.88$), which supports a linear feedforward controller calibrated from impulse-response data~\citep{astrom1995pid}.
To capture the response dynamics, we fit an LTI model to the impulse-response data of each session (Materials and Methods).

Models fit to the trial-averaged response of a random half of the trials predicted the trial-averaged response of the other half (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}C), with a pooled median held-out $R^2$ of $0.85$ across the four sessions; the median over splits ranged by session from $0.56$ in Mouse 5a (interquartile range $0.09$--$0.79$) to $0.95$ in Mouse 1b (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}D).
The spread of held-out $R^2$ within each session reflects trial-to-trial variability in the response, which we examine below.

We allowed up to five poles and four zeros, selected the order once per session on all trials, and held it fixed when scoring held-out trials (Mouse 5a, three poles and one zero; Mice 5b and 1b, four poles and three zeros; Mouse 3c, five poles and four zeros).
A two-pole model predicted held-out trials almost as well (pooled held-out $R^2 = 0.81$ against $0.85$; $0.87$ against $0.85$ in Mouse 3c).

A model fit in one session described the responses of other sessions inconsistently (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}E): although the cross-session $R^2$ was moderate on average ($0.69$, against $0.99$ within session), it ranged from $0.97$ for some session pairs to $0.12$ for others.

We conclude that we can use linear models for open loop gain design but cant reuse them across sessions. Since we have some level of similarity between sessions, we calibrate the open loop gains we can adjust them per session to fine tune using observations of trail activity (Table~\ref{tab:gains}, Materials and Methods).
The fitted poles yield two timescales (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}F).
The two modes overlap in time, so neither maps onto one feature of the response alone (in Mice 5b and 1b the slower mode contributes $60$--$68\%$ of the trough).

The dip timescale, the decay of the fastest mode (a damped 2.4--4.2\,Hz oscillation that shapes the initial suppression), was consistent across sessions (median $0.113$\,s; $0.106$--$0.114$\,s in Mice 5a, 5b and 1b, and $0.14$\,s in Mouse 3c; Materials and Methods), although it depends on model order: the one other model fitting almost as well ($R^2$ within $0.005$) gave $0.117$ instead of $0.106$\,s in Mouse 5a and $0.154$ instead of $0.114$\,s in Mouse 1b.

The rebound timescale, the slowest mode, which governs how activity returns after the dip, varied across sessions ($0.27$\,s in Mouse 1b, $0.50$\,s in Mouse 3c at the edge of the $0.5$\,s fit window, and beyond it in Mice 5a and 5b, where in Mouse 5a it adds a small sustained suppression, $6\%$ of the trough) and is correspondingly less well constrained: it exceeded the fit window in $39\%$ and $72\%$ of bootstrap refits in Mice 5a and 5b and in all refits in Mouse 3c, against $3\%$ in Mouse 1b (Materials and Methods).
Accordingly, the peak-normalized responses share the dip time course and diverge only during the rebound, which was small relative to the dip (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}D).

The dip, consistent across sessions, therefore sets how quickly stimulation can move cortical activity, whereas the session-variable rebound acts on slower timescales, at which the integral term of the controller can compensate.
Single-trial variability reflects state-dependent ongoing activity
The LTI model captured the trial-averaged response, but individual trials deviated from it, and the size of these deviations depended on brain state.

We characterized the state before each stimulus with three measures, all taken over the 1\,s before onset (Materials and Methods): motion energy from face video, a measure of the animal's movement; relative 2--4\,Hz ($\delta$) power, the fraction of 0.4--10\,Hz cortical power in the $\delta$ band, which reflects how strongly the spectrum is concentrated in slow rhythms; and absolute 2--4\,Hz power, which reflects the overall amplitude of slow fluctuations.

We quantified each trial's variability as the root-mean-square deviation of its response over the LTI fit window ($0$ to $0.5$\,s) from the trial-averaged response at its amplitude, which is the response the LTI model describes.
We normalized this variability within each session and binned trials by quartile of each state measure (1516 trials, four sessions; Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}G).
We computed the same measure over a stimulus-free window sampled between stimulus trials, to ask whether ongoing activity without stimulation shows the same state dependence (Materials and Methods).

In every session, single trials were least variable in the top motion quartile ($0.57$--$0.71$ times the session's typical trial), whereas the three lower quartiles stayed between $0.88$ and $1.30$, so the observation was a drop at the highest motion (top versus bottom quartile, geometric mean over sessions $0.58$, range $0.50$--$0.81$; Figure~\ref{fig:state_quartile}A).

Variability rose from quartile to quartile with absolute $\delta$ power in all four sessions ($2.35$, range $1.70$--$2.71$), and showed no consistent pattern with relative $\delta$ power ($1.03$, range $0.83$--$1.16$).

Ongoing activity in the stimulus-free window followed the same pattern in each state (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}G, dashed line; top versus bottom quartile $0.60$, $1.08$ and $2.70$ for motion, relative and absolute $\delta$ power), and it deviated from its own trial average about as much as the evoked response did (ratio of within-session variabilities, $0.92$--$1.06$ across sessions).

Expressed relative to the stimulus-free window, response variability changed little across quartiles (top versus bottom quartile $0.98$, $0.95$ and $0.87$; Figure~\ref{fig:state_quartile}A--C, second column); if anything, the response varied slightly less with absolute $\delta$ power than ongoing activity did.

Single-trial responses and the ongoing activity they ride on therefore changed together with state: during movement both were less variable, and with higher absolute $\delta$ power both were more variable (per-session values and supporting tests, Table~\ref{tab:stat_fig2g}).
We report this co-variation and do not separate a state-dependent change in the stimulus effect from a state-dependent change in ongoing activity.

This is consistent with brain state acting as a disturbance added to an otherwise fixed plant, which is the situation feedback control is designed to handle, and it sets a floor on how well any fixed model can predict an individual trial; we test this directly in closed loop below (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}).
The two $\delta$ measures are correlated but not redundant (Spearman $\rho = 0.47$ over the impulse trials).

We therefore carry both into the closed-loop analysis, relative power as a candidate state variable normalized for overall power and absolute power as a measure of disturbance amplitude; there, absolute power is taken over 1--4\,Hz and all state measures are computed from $-2$ to $+3$\,s around onset (Materials and Methods).

Closed-loop control improves reference-tracking accuracy
We used the PI controller (Figure~\ref{fig:figure1}E; Materials and Methods) to target spontaneous activity to $-5\%\,\Delta F/F$ for 3\,s per trial.

For each mouse, we first tuned the feedforward gain $K_r$ and the feedback gains $K_p$ and $K_i$ (Materials and Methods), and at the start of each session we adjusted them slightly to account for session specific changes.
We then ran a validation block with fixed gains, in which closed-loop trials and open-loop trials (feedforward only, no feedback) were randomly interleaved (Table~\ref{tab:gains}).
Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}A--D and F show one representative session (Mouse~2a; $K_r = 0.1$, $K_p = 0.07$, $K_i = 0.1$), and Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}E and G--I pool all 15 sessions.
On single trials, the closed-loop controller adjusted the stimulation as activity changed, whereas the open-loop input was fixed regardless of the cortical output (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}A).

As a result, trial-averaged closed-loop activity stayed close to the reference throughout stimulation, whereas open-loop activity carried the error of the feedforward calibration (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}B).
The trial-averaged closed-loop input departed from the fixed open-loop input (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}C), a correction that reflects errors in the nominal model or stimulation-related biases.
We quantified tracking accuracy on each trial as the root-mean-square error (RMSE) between activity and the reference.
In the representative session, closed loop lowered both the typical RMSE and its spread across trials (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}F).
Across sessions, closed loop kept the trial-averaged error below open loop over the whole stimulation window (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}G).

To compare sessions on one scale, we divided each session's mean closed-loop RMSE by its mean open-loop RMSE in each window, so that a ratio below one means closed loop tracked better (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}H).
We tested the log ratio across sessions with a one-sample $t$-test and checked the result in each mouse (Materials and Methods).
Over the full 3\,s window, closed loop lowered RMSE in all 15 sessions and in all 4 mice, by 23\% on average (geometric-mean ratio $0.77$, $p = 5.8\times10^{-8}$; Table~\ref{tab:stat_fig3}).
The initial deviation, the difference between output and reference at stimulation onset, settles within 1\,s.
We therefore split the stimulation window into a transient (0--1\,s), which captures this settling, and a steady state (1--3\,s), which reflects the response to ongoing disturbances.

Closed loop lowered RMSE by 15\% in the transient (ratio $0.85$; $p = 1.0\times10^{-5}$) and by 32\% in the steady state ($0.68$; $p = 4.9\times10^{-7}$), with the ratio below one in all 15 sessions and all 4 mice in both windows (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}H).
Before and after stimulation the ratio stayed at one (geometric mean $1.01$, 95\% CI $[1.00, 1.03]$, and $1.00$, $[0.98, 1.03]$).
Part of this advantage reflects the rough feedforward calibration, which left open-loop activity a median of $1.5\%\,\Delta F/F$ short of the reference during stimulation (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}B).

To separate calibration from feedback, we compared closed loop with the best fixed input, the constant command that would have minimized each session's open-loop error under the linear model, computed on the same trials, which favors open loop (Figure~\ref{fig:best_fixed}A; Materials and Methods).
This brought open-loop activity to within $0.3\%\,\Delta F/F$ of the reference and lowered its steady-state RMSE by 15\%.

Closed loop still tracked better than the best fixed input, by 13\% over the stimulation window (ratio $0.87$, $p = 6.5\times10^{-4}$; below one in 13 of 15 sessions and 3 of 4 mice), 8\% in the transient ($0.92$, $p = 0.026$) and 20\% in the steady state ($0.80$, $p = 1.4\times10^{-4}$) (Figure~\ref{fig:best_fixed}B,C; Table~\ref{tab:stat_fig3}).
Feedback also moved the average command toward this input on its own.

The mean closed-loop command was 1.16 times the open-loop command (median over sessions), against 1.28 times for the best fixed input, and the two were correlated across sessions (Spearman $\rho = 0.67$, $p = 0.0081$, Figure~\ref{fig:best_fixed}D).
Under the same model, recalibration leaves across-trial variance unchanged, so the variance reduction below is not a calibration effect.
Closed-loop control reduces trial-to-trial variability
In the representative session, across-trial variance was similar in the two conditions before stimulation but diverged upon stimulation onset (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}D).
Open-loop variance reduced slightly, whereas closed-loop variance was significantly reduced, because feedback acts on each trial's deviation in real time.
Averaged across all 15 sessions, we observe the drop in variance during stimulation holds showing its not a session specific effect (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}E).

In the per-session ratio of closed- to open-loop across-trial variance (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}I; same test as above), closed loop lowered variance by 42\% over the stimulation window (ratio $0.58$; $p = 6.3\times10^{-6}$; 14 of 15 sessions, all 4 mice), by 33\% in the transient ($0.67$; $p = 5.5\times10^{-4}$) and by 46\% in the steady state ($0.54$; $p = 1.3\times10^{-6}$).

Before and after stimulation, the ratio stayed near one (geometric mean $1.04$, 95\% CI $[0.91, 1.18]$, and $1.05$, $[0.93, 1.19]$), so the reduction was confined to the period in which feedback was active, showing that trials were sampled from similar distributions in both cases.

This is consistent with disturbance rejection: feedback cancels part of the ongoing activity that differs from trial to trial, which we interpret as input from other brain areas or external stimuli and the controller treats them as disturbance to the local dynamics.
The size of the improvement varied across sessions, likely reflecting differences in arousal, opsin expression and the overlap between the stimulated and recorded regions.

Controller performance is brain-state dependent
How well feedback tracked the reference depended on brain state.

We described each trial's state with four variables: the initial deviation of activity from the reference at onset, motion energy, 2--4\,Hz power relative to 0.4--10\,Hz power, and absolute 1--4\,Hz power.
Motion and power were measured from 2\,s before onset to the end of stimulation (Materials and Methods).
Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}A shows closed-loop trials, each high in one state.
Face video was available for 11 of the 15 sessions; the other 4 were excluded from all motion analyses.
Within closed-loop trials, different states mattered in the two windows (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}B,C).

We regressed each trial's tracking error (RMSE) on the state variables within each of the 11 sessions with face video and measured how much of its trial-to-trial variation each variable explained beyond the others; the two power measures are correlated, so each entered its own model with the initial deviation and motion (Materials and Methods).
The initial deviation explained much of the variation in transient error but almost none in the steady state.

Absolute 1--4\,Hz power explained a modest part in both windows, more than any other variable in the steady state, and remained the largest when relative power was added to the same model (Figure~\ref{fig:f4_exemplars}B,C).
Relative power explained little, and motion explained nothing beyond the other variables.
Closed-loop error thus varied with large, slow fluctuations but not with motion.

We then compared open- and closed-loop tracking across the range of each state, fitting steady-state RMSE against the state within each session and testing the slopes across sessions (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}D; 15 sessions from 4 mice, or 11 for motion; Materials and Methods).
We summarized each state with three slopes, each per within-session standard deviation (SD) of the state.
The open-loop slope measures \emph{predictability}: a positive slope means that error rises with the state in a way a fixed feedforward input cannot anticipate, which we treat as a disturbance.
The closed-loop slope measures \emph{regularizability}: a flat slope means that feedback tracks the reference regardless of the state.

Closed-loop alone cannot characterize the effect of state on improvement of ability to control over open loop, as the open-loop could also be just as effective if disturbances are perturbing the trial.

We therefore also measured \emph{attenuation}, the change with state in the error ratio, the fraction of open-loop error left under feedback; a falling ratio means that feedback removes proportionally more error as the state grows.

Each slope is its own question; Table~\ref{tab:fig4_state_stats} gives every estimate with its $p$ value and, as a check, a Holm-adjusted value, under which the motion attenuation and the closed-loop slope on absolute power remain significant.
Closed loop lowered error across the range of every state, and two states stood out.

Feedback attenuated the error that accompanied motion: the more the animal moved, the more of the error feedback removed (the error ratio fell by 13\% per SD, $p = 0.0023$, in all 11 sessions and all 4 mice).
Open-loop error rose with motion ($p = 0.011$) while closed-loop error stayed flat ($p = 0.16$).

Absolute 1--4\,Hz power raised closed-loop error in all 15 sessions and all 4 mice ($p = 7.1\times10^{-4}$) and open-loop error by a similar amount ($p = 0.0098$), so feedback did not hold the output at the reference as this power grew; the fraction of error left under feedback did not change significantly ($+7\%$ per SD, $p = 0.094$).

The initial deviation raised closed-loop error ($p = 0.014$); its effect on open-loop error was of similar size but not significant ($p = 0.056$), and their ratio did not change ($p = 0.91$), so feedback removed the same fraction of error whether a trial began far from or near the reference.

Relative 2--4\,Hz power raised closed-loop error slightly ($p = 0.035$) but not open-loop error ($p = 0.98$), so the fraction of error left under feedback rose with it ($+5\%$ per SD, $p = 0.029$); these effects are small.
The power measures span the stimulation period, so they describe activity during stimulation, which the loop itself shapes, rather than the state in which the trial began.

Absolute 1--4\,Hz power, which indexes large, slow fluctuations, therefore accounted for more of the variation in steady-state closed-loop error than any other state (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}C), and feedback did not hold the output at the reference as it grew.
Feedback partly rejects a disturbance predicted from the contralateral hemisphere
To test disturbance rejection directly, we estimated each trial's disturbance from the opposite hemisphere.

A linear predictor from contralateral pixels to the ipsilateral control readout was fit only on spontaneous, no-laser frames, so it learned how the two hemispheres covary but nothing about the stimulation (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}E).
It generalized to held-out frames ($R^2 = 0.75$ in the session of Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}F; median $0.76$, range $0.44$--$0.98$, 13 sessions).

On a stimulation trial, the prediction gave the \emph{Global} component $G$, an estimate of what the site would have done without controller input, and the remainder of the measured response $A$ gave the \emph{Local} component $L = A - G$, what the laser and controller added on top of $G$ (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}F).
The split is a linear projection, not a causal decomposition.

The predictor was blind to the laser but its input was not: contralateral activity also changed during stimulation, so $G$ carried part of the laser response (median $23\%$ of the readout's open-loop dip over 0--3\,s).
After subtracting the session's average leak and referencing $G$ to its pre-onset baseline, we took the remaining trial-to-trial excursion as the disturbance $D$ (Materials and Methods).

We scored rejection with a rejection ratio (RR), the residual energy of the response about the reference divided by the energy of $D$, both over the steady-state window; $\mathrm{RR} < 1$ indicates rejection.
Of the 13 sessions with a predictor, we excluded two in which a standing offset supplied more than one third of the closed-loop residual energy ($38\%$ and $59\%$; Materials and Methods).

In the remaining 11, closed loop partly rejected the disturbance (session-level mixed model, geometric-mean RR $0.58$, one-sided $p = 1.3\times10^{-4}$; 595 trials, 3 mice; session median below one in all 11; Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}G; Table~\ref{tab:stat_fig4g}).

Open loop, by contrast, left more residual energy than the disturbance it faced (median session RR $1.25$, against $0.72$ in closed loop; lower in closed loop in all 11 sessions, $p = 4.9\times10^{-4}$).
Most of this difference lay in the response level, which open loop sets only by calibration.

The standing offset supplied a median $35\%$ of the residual energy in open loop and $7\%$ in closed loop ($p = 9.8\times10^{-4}$), whereas the fluctuation energy fell less, from $0.66$ to $0.54$ of the disturbance energy ($p = 0.0024$; both lower in closed loop in 10 of 11 sessions).

A model-predictive controller optimizes reference tracking on data replay
The PI controller corrects instantaneous error but is blind to incoming disturbances.
A model-predictive controller (MPC;~\citealp{rawlings2017model}) uses a model that predicts how activity will respond to stimulation, given its recent history.

At every frame, it solves a constrained optimization for the stimulation sequence over the next second that best tracks the reference while penalizing abrupt command changes, applies the first command, and replans at the next frame (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}A,B).
Replanning from each new measurement lets it correct for disturbances its model did not predict.

Its predictions came from a linear vector autoregressive model with exogenous input (VARX;~\citealp{lutkepohl2005new}) built from the past second of the controlled site, 100 sites over the cortex and the stimulation.

On held-out open-loop trials the VARX predicted the controlled site better than the last observed value for a short horizon forward in time, and the 100 cortical sites improved on a model of the site and laser alone (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}H; Figure~\ref{fig:supp_varx}).
Running MPC in real time needs new software and hardware on the rig with lower latency, so we replayed recorded closed-loop trials with the MPC in place of the PI controller.
Each replay drove a VARX fitted to the whole session with the trial's recorded one-step prediction residuals (Materials and Methods).
We used this model to predict activity over a short horizon (Figure~\ref{fig:supp_varx}).
The MPC's own model never saw a closed-loop trial.
All results in this section are descriptive simulations.

In one session with a constant reference (Mouse~1e), the MPC lowered the median per-trial RMSE over the steady-state window (1--3\,s) from $1.46$ under the recorded PI controller to $0.88\%\,\Delta F/F$, and its RMSE was lower on 107 of 108 trials (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}C--E).
Across-trial variance over the same window fell by $37\%$ (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}F), and the RMSE gain held across the command-smoothness penalties we tried (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}G).
With perfect prediction (the replay model and the trial's future residuals), the MPC's median per-trial RMSE over the same window improved to $0.27\%\,\Delta F/F$.
The input constraints thus imposed only a small performance limit; most of the MPC's residual error was prediction error, from plant--model mismatch and unforecastable disturbance.
With the sinusoidal reference the MPC lowered the error.

We replayed the 57 CL$+$p trials of the representative session of Figure~\ref{fig:figure5} (Mouse~3b), the controller mode that, like the MPC, combined feedback with advance knowledge of the reference.
Median per-trial RMSE over the 4\,s window fell from $3.00$ under CL$+$p to $2.67\%\,\Delta F/F$, and the MPC's RMSE was lower on 56 of 57 trials (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}I--K).

Across-trial variance fell to $0.71$ times that of CL$+$p (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}L), and as with preview the phase lag stayed near zero, against $71^\circ$ under open loop (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}M).
In both replays, predicting the disturbance lowered the error that feedback left, and in the sinusoidal replay also its trial-to-trial variability.

Discussion
A cortical region's response to local optogenetic inhibition was approximately linear and time-invariant on average, but single trials varied with brain state and ongoing activity.
A proportional--integral controller that assumed this linear, time-invariant model tracked the reference and reduced trial-to-trial variability on average by correcting deviations from it.
Its single-trial performance depended on brain state, consistent with disturbances that vary with state.
Replayed on recorded trials, a model-predictive controller that forecast the disturbance lowered the error further.
The impulse experiments set our design choices.
The trial-averaged response grew monotonically with laser power, and a low-order linear model fitted each session's average (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}B--D), so the controller assumed linearity.

The fitted models transferred only inconsistently between sessions (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}E), so we used them only for a rough feedforward gain, carried it over between sessions with small adjustments, and let feedback correct the rest.
The best fixed input was a median of 1.28 times the command this gain produced, and the closed-loop command moved toward that input on its own (Figure~\ref{fig:best_fixed}D).
Single trials also varied with state (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}G), but what counts as brain state differs between studies.
It can be the activity at stimulus onset, which shaped optogenetic responses in macaque sensorimotor cortex~\citep{bryan2025temporal} and enters our analysis as the initial deviation.

It can also be a variable that changes the dynamics themselves, such as movement and arousal~\citep{Niell2010,Vinck2015,McGinley2015waking} or the synchrony of ongoing activity~\citep{Poulet2008,Harris2011}, which our slow-wave power measures track.
These variables shape the dynamics but are hard to predict, so we measured them post hoc, though identifying them in real time could inform the controller, as we plan next.

Sorted by movement or slow-wave power, single trials departed from their average about as much as stimulus-free activity did from its own, with similar state dependence (Figure~\ref{fig:state_quartile}), consistent with a fixed response riding on ongoing activity~\citep{Arieli1996,Shimaoka2019}.
State that adds an offset is a disturbance that feedback subtracts, whereas state that changes gain is a model error that feedback must tolerate.

Models that treat state as a parameter of the dynamics switch between linear systems~\citep{linderman2017rslds} or model dynamics within a regime, such as the subspace relevant to a behavior~\citep{sani2021modeling}.
Input--output models fitted per state would separate offset from gain, but would require precise identification of each state switch and, for control, ideally its forecast.

A real-time decoder of discrete cortical states, such as a hidden semi-Markov model of LFP spectra in mouse somatosensory cortex~\citep{weiss2024realtime}, labels the state without modelling the response to stimulation, so it could select among interpretable per-state models, although its estimates lag offline ones by about 120--240\,ms.

All such models must contend with inputs they cannot observe, as cortical activity tracks uninstructed movements~\citep{musall2019single,stringer2019spontaneous} and drive from other areas~\citep{zagha2013motor,harris2013topdown} as well as its own dynamics.
We therefore simplified, treating the trial-averaged system as stationary (Assumption~\ref{assm:trial_avg}).
A single linear model is then enough for control if, within a session, the laser's average effect on the readout is well defined and monotonic.
The distribution of states is unknown, and over-sampling one state shifts the average toward that state's mean response but not beyond the range of the per-state means.
That range, unmeasured here, loosely bounds the design model's error.

Averages therefore need enough trials, and in three sessions the cross-trial variance of spontaneous activity changed by only 1--2\% with the number of trials averaged (Figure~\ref{fig:spatial_spread}C).

A nonlinear model is the usual alternative, but linear ones often predict brain activity, including responses to stimulation, about as well~\citep{Nozari2024,sani2024dissociative,Yang2021}, and the richer the model of the dynamics, the more must be known to control with it.

Both kinds forecast ongoing activity only briefly, and stimulus-blind, univariate forecasts of spontaneous mouse wide-field activity stay informative for about 1.5\,s, with deep models modestly ahead of a linear autoregressive one~\citep{lu2025benchmarking}.

Part of this limit cannot be removed, because brain activity has random sources and depends on unobserved processes such as neuromodulation, so even a perfect forecasting model would leave some error~\citep{lueckmann2025zapbench}.
Feedback partly opposes such unforecastable inputs through the error they cause.

A model for feedback design need only capture how the laser moves the readout~\citep{gevers2005identification}, and a low-order linear model makes stability, gain limits and bandwidth computable~\citep{astrom2008feedback}.
Proportional--integral control needs only the sign of the laser's effect, which was consistently suppressive (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}B; Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}B).
The simplest optimal regulator of a system must model it~\citep{conant1970every}, and ours modelled only its average.

The feedforward gain approximately inverted the average response, and the integrator, an internal model of a constant signal rather than of cortex, drives a constant offset toward zero within its clamp~\citep{francis1976internal}.

Monotonicity gives each attainable reference one steady-state light drive, which low-gain integral control of an exponentially stable linear plant reaches despite a saturating actuator and input delay~\citep{logemann2000absolute}.
Session-to-session variability therefore limits the gains, not whether some correctly signed gain stabilizes the loop~\citep{morari1985robust}.

With this minimal model, feedback lowered error in every session and, on average, trial-to-trial variability (Figure~\ref{fig:figure3}H,I), and about half of the error reduction remained against the best fixed input.

Against the contralaterally predicted disturbance~\citep{Shimaoka2019,Ye2026}, feedback lowered residual energy in all 11 retained sessions (two excluded for large closed-loop offsets), mostly by shrinking the standing offset left by open-loop calibration, while fluctuations fell less (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}G; Table~\ref{tab:stat_fig4g}).

Earlier closed-loop optogenetic controllers held neuronal firing rates in culture and in rodent thalamus~\citep{newman2015optogenetic,bolus2018design,bolus2021state}, clamped single-neuron calcium signals~\citep{Zhang2018} or phase-locked light to oscillations~\citep{nicholson2018analogue,kanta2019closed,Zaaimi2022}.

In anesthetized rat thalamus, proportional--integral feedback held firing rates although its fitted model predicted open-loop responses poorly, lowered Fano factors below open loop in five cells, and could not lower rates above target with an excitatory opsin~\citep{bolus2018design}, the mirror image of our one-sided limit.

Closest to our readout, on/off two-photon feedback in awake mouse cortex held the calcium signal of single neurons near set levels, with a mean absolute error of about 5\%\,$\Delta F/F$, and made optogenetic responses more uniform across cells and trials~\citep{Zhang2018}, whereas our controller graded the light continuously and regulated a mesoscale signal.

Changing brain state was anticipated as a disturbance~\citep{bolus2021state} or a change in the plant~\citep{grosenick2015closed}, whereas here we related residual closed-loop error to measured state.

Poorly regulated trials may reflect activity outside the controller's model, so per-trial error probes brain state: slow 1--4\,Hz power explained part of the 1--3\,s error, and movement none (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}B,C).
Open-loop error rose with movement while closed-loop error stayed flat.
Slow, large-amplitude 1--4\,Hz fluctuations were reduced, but closed-loop error still rose with their power as much as open-loop error (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}D; Table~\ref{tab:fig4_state_stats}).

An effective delay of 37--61\,ms (loop delay at most 47\,ms and about half that on average, Figure~\ref{fig:figure1}F, plus the 14\,ms half-sample hold) caps the feedback bandwidth at about 2.6--4\,Hz by the crossover criterion $\omega_c\tau \lesssim 1$\,rad~\citep{skogestad2005multivariable}.
Cortical lag (Figure~\ref{fig:figure5}H) probably lowers the unmeasured crossover further.
Large slow excursions may also saturate the command, which can suppress activity but not raise it.
A closed- to open-loop error spectrum and time at the ceiling would separate delay from saturation.
The band-power window spans stimulation, which the loop shapes, and motion and slow power are anticorrelated~\citep{McGinley2015waking}, so state effects are associations.

Where state changes the plant itself, the alternative to a single time-invariant model is a context-dependent model whose controller switches, or schedules its gains, with state~\citep{rugh2000research,grosenick2015closed}.

Adaptive deep brain stimulation switches on when a measured biomarker crosses a threshold~\citep{little2013adaptive}, rather than adjusting stimulation continuously, and optogenetic feedback in mouse thalamus paired a first-order model with an adaptive estimator that compensated for mismatch online~\citep{bolus2021state}.

Model-predictive control is a modest step beyond proportional--integral control, adding prediction to a linear model that now includes the rest of cortex and treating the one-sided laser as a constraint~\citep{mayne2000constrained}.
Preview, which predicts only the reference, already cancelled the cortical phase lag that feedback left (Figure~\ref{fig:figure5}H).
The contralateral hemisphere predicted much of the site's spontaneous activity (Figure~\ref{fig:figure4}F).

Yet in one session, 100 cortical sites added little to a 200\,ms forecast of the site beyond its own past and the laser (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}H; Figure~\ref{fig:supp_varx}E), so drive from the rest of cortex was observable but largely unforecastable at short leads.
A linear model without subcortical signals may understate what is forecastable.
In a replay of one session, the controller lowered the error that feedback left by about 40\%, and by about 80\% given the future residuals (Figure~\ref{fig:mpc_direct}C--F).
What remained was mostly activity its model could not predict.

The replayed cortex shares the controller's model class and responds to the laser identically in every state, so these values bound, rather than measure, live performance, as for model-based designs for electrical stimulation tested in simulation~\citep{Yang2018,Yang2021}.
A live controller should keep integral action~\citep{pannocchia2003disturbance}.
The data comprise four impulse sessions in three mice, 15 separate controller sessions in four mice (11 in the disturbance analysis) and three sinusoidal sessions in one mouse.

In every impulse session the average response grew monotonically with power and was predicted by a linear model (Figure~\ref{fig:figure2}B--D), so with a comparable preparation it should be predictable enough for control.

All sessions inhibited one somatosensory site in awake, head-fixed mice, leaving excitation, other areas and task performance untested, though the preparation reaches all dorsal cortex~\citep{Matveev2024}.

Inhibition spreads toward the adjacent readout (Figure~\ref{fig:spatial_spread}A,B;~\citealp{li2019spatiotemporal}), in this setup though we only show control over the kernel, extension to wide bran activity can be derived in future work.
Interleaved trials limit, but cannot remove, drift in brain state between conditions.

Gains were tuned empirically, and the low-gain guarantee is asymptotic and assumes a fixed plant, whereas our integrator ran over 3\,s trials and was reset between them, so the theory motivates the design and stability rests on the observation that no session showed sustained oscillation.

We present a procedure for precise feedback control that makes cortical activity follow a chosen reference without an explicit model of its dynamics: if brief stimuli at several intensities evoke a monotonic average response that a low-order linear model fits, and the trial average is stable in the number of trials (Assumption~\ref{assm:trial_avg}), proportional--integral control with feedforward compensation, tuned to the experiment, can be used.

Nothing in it is specific to wide-field imaging or optogenetics, so it should carry over to two-photon imaging, electrophysiology, electrocorticography or functional MRI, and to electrical stimulation, within each readout's bandwidth.
Model-predictive control may add precision where the disturbance is partly predictable.
A site that tracks a chosen reference also lets its influence on dorsal cortex, striatum~\citep{Peters2021} or behavior~\citep{ZatkaHaas2021} be tested at defined activity levels.

As in the voltage clamp and the optoclamp~\citep{newman2015optogenetic}, the laser command needed to track the reference should then report the drive that the loop opposes, a prediction we did not test.

Illumination was as in \citet{Matveev2024}, where it did not detectably activate the opsin.

An infrared camera filmed the face and forepaws during a subset of sessions, synchronized with imaging as in \citet{Matveev2024}.

Real-time control
The control loop ran as a dedicated real-time process, triggered by each blue frame and managed separately from display and disk writing.
End-to-end latency, from camera exposure to stimulation command, was measured over 200 loop cycles (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure1}F).

Over a whole session (Mouse~4; 3539 closed-loop laser updates, timed from the exposure start of the source frame to the laser edge recorded on the Timeline), latency had a median of 24.0\,ms, a 99th percentile of 40.0\,ms and a maximum of 43.5\,ms, and 12.6\% of updates arrived after the next blue frame.
\emph{Online signal.} The feedback signal was the mean fluorescence in a $10 \times 10$ pixel square (0.173\,mm on a side) centered on the readout site in somatosensory cortex.

Offline, we re-extracted this signal from the compressed movie.

Inter-trial intervals were 15\,s plus a uniform random jitter of up to 1\,s, so that laser onset times were not predictable and did not entrain adaptation.
No light was applied between trials.
The reference was held at $y_{\mathrm{ref}} = -5\%\,\Delta F/F$ throughout the stimulation window, a suppression of five percentage points below the running baseline.
Each session began with a tuning phase (\nameref{sec:gain_opt}), followed by a validation block of 30--200 trials (Table~\ref{tab:gains}).

In eight sessions of Mouse~1 (1a, 1c--1f, 1h, 1j and 1k) the logged starts drifted relative to the recorded laser command, by up to 7 frames (0.2\,s).

In these sessions we re-derived each open-loop onset from the rise of its recorded command, minus the fixed lag between the logged start and the first command in the sessions without drift (1.9 frames: one frame of trial bookkeeping plus the loop latency), so that time zero means the same in every session.

We checked every corrected session by eye against the command and the evoked response.
