Model-predictive control replay
We simulated a model-predictive controller (MPC) on one closed-loop session (Mouse~1e; 108 closed-loop trials).

Activity at the controlled site and at 100 sites over dorsal cortex, with the laser command as input, was modeled as a linear vector autoregressive process with exogenous input (VARX; 35 lags, 1\,s, of every channel and of the laser command; construction and held-out prediction in Fig.~\ref{fig:supp_varx}).
The 100 sites were an evenly spaced grid of $5 \times 5$ pixel boxes over the brain mask.
The VARX was fitted by ridge regression.
The penalty (100) and the history length were checked on validation data over $10$--$10^{4}$ and 5--35 frames, where prediction was nearly flat (Fig.~\ref{fig:supp_varx}D).

At every frame the MPC chose the laser commands over a 1\,s horizon that minimized the squared deviation of the predicted controlled signal from the reference, plus a penalty ($\lambda = 0.1$) on command changes and a small penalty pulling the command toward the median recorded closed-loop command.
Commands were bounded between 0 and the largest command the rig delivered.
The MPC applied the first command and planned again at the next frame.
To replay a trial, we drove the VARX fitted to the whole session with that trial's recorded one-step residuals.
Under the recorded laser this reproduces the recorded trial exactly, so the PI baseline is the trial as it ran and needs no model of the PI loop.
The model was trained on the session's spontaneous and open-loop frames only, so no closed-loop trial, including the one being replayed, entered its training.
As a bound, we also replayed each trial with the MPC given the actual data instead of model's prediction (perfect prediction).
RMSE was scored over the steady-state window (1--3\,s).

We repeated the replay on the 57 CL$+$p trials of the representative sinusoidal session of Fig.~\ref{fig:figure5} (Mouse~3b), with the 1\,Hz reference in the MPC cost over its horizon, and scored RMSE over the 4\,s window.
Here too the MPC's model was fitted without any closed-loop (CL or CL$+$p) trial, on spontaneous and open-loop frames, with the replayed trial's fold (one of five) also held out.
All MPC results are descriptive.
System characterization
Impulse responses and evoked suppression
Impulse experiments were run open loop with the same imaging.
Each stimulus was a single pulse about one imaging frame long (23--28\,ms), separated by randomized intervals (median 5.7--9.8\,s across sessions).
Responses were read out offline from the hemodynamically corrected movie over the readout region, normalized as in \emph{Two $\Delta F/F$ normalizations}.
To test whether the input--output relation was linear and monotonic, we delivered stimuli at three to nine nonzero amplitudes per session, up to 1.6\,mW, in pseudorandom order.
Every nonzero amplitude had at least 44 trials.
We summarized each response by its mean $\Delta F/F$ over the 200\,ms after onset (evoked suppression),
where $j$ indexes trials and $W$ spans the eight samples from onset to 200\,ms.
Each trial's trace is referenced to its value at the onset sample, so $y_{j,t_{\mathrm{on}}} = 0$.
We use the window mean because it is less sensitive to single-sample noise than the trough.
We regressed mean evoked suppression on amplitude to test linearity.

\emph{Spatial extent.} We mapped the trial-averaged $\Delta F/F$ across the imaged cortex at each amplitude and counted pixels whose background-subtracted response fell below 50\% of the median response within 0.2\,mm of the peak at the strongest amplitude.
Background was estimated per amplitude from an annulus 0.6--0.9\,mm from the peak, which removes the global hemodynamic component.
Areas use the 17.3\,\textmu m pixel size (Fig.~\ref{fig:spatial_spread}A,B).
Transfer-function fitting
We fitted a continuous-time transfer function to each session's amplitude-normalized impulse response.

The trial-averaged response at each amplitude $a$ was divided by $a$, and these normalized responses were averaged with weights proportional to $a^{2}$, so that the high signal-to-noise amplitudes set the dynamics, giving $h(t)$ over the 0.5\,s after onset.
Under linearity the normalized responses coincide, so the fit itself tests the linear assumption.

We fitted $h(t)$ by prediction-error minimization, sweeping 1--5 poles, 0--4 zeros (strictly proper, so $h(0) = 0$) and 0--3 samples of pure delay (0--85.7\,ms), and selected the order by the Akaike Information Criterion.
When the selected model reproduced $h(t)$ with $R^{2} < 0.98$, we instead took the model with the fewest parameters among those within 0.002 of the best $R^{2}$.
In one session (Mouse 3c), whose onset-referenced response stayed offset from zero, no order fitted well from the default initialization (best $R^2 = 0.94$).
We therefore added, in every session, one candidate initialized from a fit to the baseline-referenced response plus one pole near the origin.
It was selected only in Mouse 3c (five poles, four zeros, $R^{2} = 0.99$).
The near-origin pole contributes less than 0.2\% of the response and is not interpreted.
Held-out refits rebuilt this initialization from training trials only.
\emph{Held-out validation} (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}C,D).
For each of 100 random splits, trials were divided in half within each amplitude, so that both halves span the full dose range.
We rebuilt $h(t)$ on one half, refitted the model at the session's selected order, and scored its prediction against the other half, in both directions (200 folds).
The prediction carries the model's own gain, so a gain mismatch counts against it.
We report the median and interquartile range of held-out $R^{2}$ over the folds whose refit succeeded (90\% in Mouse 3c, at least 98\% elsewhere).
The pooled value is the median over all such folds of the four sessions.
Model order was selected once on all trials and is not itself cross-validated.
\emph{Cross-session model swap} (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}E).
Entry $(i,j)$ is the $R^{2}$ of session $i$'s fitted unit response against session $j$'s measured $h(t)$, after a single least-squares gain for that pair.
The free gain restricts the comparison to the shape of the response, which a controller cannot re-tune.
The diagonal is each model's in-sample fit.
\emph{Time constants} (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}F).
Each continuous-time pole $p$ gives $\tau = -1/\mathrm{Re}(p)$.
We report the fastest (dip) and slowest (rebound) modes per session.
A time constant longer than the 0.5\,s fit window is not resolved by the fit and is drawn at the window edge.

To check identifiability, we refitted 300 bootstrap resamples of trials within amplitude, each rebuilding $h(t)$ and refitting at the selected order, and computed the fraction of refits whose slowest $\tau$ exceeded the fit window (18 samples, 0--0.49\,s), counting failed refits (fewer than 3\%) as not exceeding it.
This fraction was large in three of four sessions (Results), so we show no intervals.
Controller tuning
We scored tracking by the root-mean-squared deviation from the reference.
For trial $i$, with the errors over the evaluation window collected in $e_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{T}$,
so values carry the units of $\Delta F/F$, and the cost of a gain pair $K$ is the mean of per-trial RMSE over its $N$ trials.
We used three named evaluation windows.
The \textbf{full stimulation window}, $t = 0$ to $+3$\,s, was used for per-trial and cross-session RMSE.

Within it, the \textbf{transient window}, $t = 0$ to $+1$\,s, covers the approach to the reference after the laser-evoked inhibitory deflection, and the \textbf{steady-state window}, $t = +1$ to $+3$\,s, covers the interval over which the controller tracks the reference.
The 1\,s boundary is a fixed convention, about five times the $\sim$200\,ms impulse dip.

The steady-state window excludes the laser-evoked transient, and it alone was used for the state dependence and disturbance rejection of Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4} (panels D and G; panel C reports both windows) and for the constant-reference MPC replay.
\emph{Gain grid.} Gradients of the cost require a model, so we mapped the cost surface directly.
In one session (Mouse~1g) the controller cycled through 10 fixed PI gain pairs, and we estimated $\hat{J}(K)$ at each node over the full window (Fig.~\ref{fig:cost_landscape}A,D).
The minimum fell at $(K_p, K_i) = (0.05,\,0.10)$, with $\hat{J} = 16.1$.
We read the grid as showing a smooth cost surface with a low-cost basin, not as locating a global optimum.

\emph{Online gain search.} In a second session of the same mouse (136 trials), the controller tuned its own gains during the experiment with the zeroth-order search of Algorithm~\ref{alg:zo}, starting from open loop ($K_p = K_i = 0$).
A candidate replaced the current gains only if it lowered the running best cost.
The online cost was evaluated over the stimulation window less two samples, so its values are not comparable with the grid.

Two candidates were accepted, lowering the online cost from 16.6 to 12.3, and the search ended at $(K_p, K_i) = (0.07,\,0.06)$, inside the low-cost region of the grid (Fig.~\ref{fig:cost_landscape}A--C).
We report this run as a feasibility demonstration, not as a reliable optimizer.
\emph{Gains used for validation.} For each mouse, initial gains were set by hand within the range the grid had explored, starting from the least-squares $K_r$ of Eq.~\eqref{eq:kr}.
Later sessions, including the first sessions of Mice 2 and 4, which had no impulse session, started from the gains of earlier sessions, with small adjustments at the start of each session.
Gains were then held fixed for the validation block (Table~\ref{tab:gains}).
Session and trial selection
All exclusions are collected here.
\emph{Motion.}
No trial was excluded on motion.
Motion enters the analyses only as a state variable.
\emph{Behavioral video.}
Motion analyses used the 11 of 15 sessions with a usable motion trace (1190 trials).
\emph{Predictor availability.}
The disturbance analysis (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}E--G) needs a contralateral predictor, which could be fitted in 13 of the 15 sessions.
The other two lacked a usable full-frame recording aligned to the control readout.
No session was excluded on predictor quality.
We report the predictor's held-out performance instead.
\emph{Standing setpoint offset.}

For the disturbance-rejection analysis only, we excluded sessions whose closed-loop response stayed above the reference throughout stimulation, because the rejection ratio would count that standing offset as unrejected disturbance.

Over the steady-state window the residual energy splits exactly into $\overline{(A-r)^{2}} = (\bar{A}-r)^{2} + \mathrm{var}(A)$, and we excluded a session when the first term, the standing offset, supplied more than one third of the total.
This removed sessions 1c and 4 (Table~\ref{tab:gains}).

In these two sessions the closed-loop average sat $2.2$ and $1.4\,\%\,\Delta F/F$ above the reference, and the offset supplied $38\%$ and $59\%$ of the residual energy, against $17\%$ or less in each of the other eleven.
We chose the threshold after inspecting the sessions.
Any threshold between 20\% and 37\% selects the same eleven.
Brain-state measures
We characterized cortical state on each trial with up to four quantities.
The impulse analysis (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}G) and the controller analysis (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}) measure them over different windows, deliberately, because they ask different questions.

The \emph{initial deviation} (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4} only) is the absolute distance of the readout from the reference at the onset sample, $\lvert y(t_{\mathrm{on}}) - r \rvert$, with $r = -5\%\,\Delta F/F$.
It measures how far from target a trial starts.

\emph{Motion energy} is the mean over the window of the z-scored motion signal (Behavioral monitoring): the mean, not the mean square, of the z-score, because the square is smallest for trials near the session mean and would rank unusually still trials alongside active ones.
\emph{Relative 2--4\,Hz power} is the ratio of band power in 2--4\,Hz, the sub-band least attenuated by the controller, to total power in 0.4--10\,Hz.
The ratio avoids the confound that any absolute spectral measure co-varies with the overall magnitude of the signal, which differs between conditions by construction.
\emph{Absolute low-frequency power} is band power without that normalization: 2--4\,Hz in Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}G and $\log_{10}$ of 1--4\,Hz power in Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}.
We report it alongside the relative measure because a factor that acts through the amplitude of ongoing activity shows in the absolute measure only.
\emph{Windows.} In Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}G, motion, relative and absolute power are taken over the same strictly pre-stimulus window, $[-1, 0)$\,s, the 35 samples before onset.

An impulse is a single brief input, so the question there is how the state in which the stimulus arrives alters its response, and a pre-stimulus window measures that state without overlapping the 0--200\,ms response.

In Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4} all three are taken over one common window, $[-2, +3)$\,s, the 175 samples from 2\,s before onset to the end of stimulation, because tracking performance depends both on the state a trial begins in and on activity that develops while the controller acts.
These measures therefore describe concurrent activity rather than a pre-stimulus state.
The effect of feedback is assessed through the open- versus closed-loop contrast, in which both conditions are measured identically.

\emph{Spectral estimation.} In Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}G each 35-sample segment was mean-subtracted and Hann-tapered, and band power was the sum of the one-sided periodogram over the native 1\,Hz bins inside the band, edges inclusive.
In Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4} each 175-sample segment $x$ was linearly detrended, Hann-tapered with window $w$ and zero-padded to at least 8192 points, giving the one-sided spectral density
with the integral evaluated by the trapezoid rule between the exact band edges.

Integrating between exact edges makes the measure independent of segment length (Spearman $\rho = 0.9999$ across 174-, 175- and 176-sample windows), which summing native bins is not: at 0.2\,Hz resolution a one-sample change moves the nominal band edges.
\emph{Quartile display} (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}D).

We binned each session's trials into quartiles of that session's state distribution (open- and closed-loop trials together), z-scored per-trial RMSE within session using the pooled open- and closed-loop distribution, averaged it within each quartile and condition, and averaged these session means across sessions (mean $\pm$ SEM).
Pooling the conditions for the z-score keeps the level difference between them while removing session-to-session differences in scale.
The test of state dependence is the per-session slope analysis under \nameref{sec:stats}.
State exemplars and error decomposition

To ask which state accounts for closed-loop tracking error, and when within the trial, we analyzed the closed-loop trials of the 11 sessions with motion capture (613 trials; 16 to 108 per session) one session at a time.
The outcome was per-trial RMSE in the transient and steady-state windows.
The four state measures were z-scored within session, with absolute power entered as its logarithm.
For each session and window we fitted ordinary least-squares models with an intercept and report each factor's \emph{unique} $R^2$, the drop in adjusted $R^2$ when that factor is removed,
for a model with $p$ factors fitted to $n$ trials.
Adjusted $R^2$ removes the positive floor that in-sample $R^2$ differences have at these trial counts.
Relative and absolute power are correlated, and in one four-factor model one would absorb the variance the other shares with it.

In Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}C each power measure therefore enters its own three-factor model on the same base, $\{\text{initial deviation}, \text{motion}, \text{relative}\}$ and $\{\text{initial deviation}, \text{motion}, \text{absolute}\}$.
The unique $R^2$ of initial deviation and motion are taken from the first.
We report the mean and SEM over sessions.
Fig.~\ref{fig:f4_exemplars}B--D repeats the decomposition with both power terms in one model, and with each alone.
The exemplar trials (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}A) illustrate each state as cleanly as the data allow.

With $z_{ij}$ the value of state $j$ on trial $i$, z-scored over the trials from which the exemplar is drawn, the exemplar for state $j$ is the trial that maximizes $z_{ij} - \max_{k \neq j} z_{ik}$ among trials with $z_{ij} > 1$ (or, if none exceeds 1, the trial with the largest $z_{ij}$).
Exemplars are drawn from the pool for Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}A and within each session for Fig.~\ref{fig:f4_exemplars}A.
Impulse-response variability and brain state
For Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}G we asked whether brain state changes how far a single impulse response departs from the trial average.

Any fixed amplitude-to-response model, the LTI model included, predicts the same response for every trial at a given amplitude, so we took as each trial's variability the root-mean-square distance between its response and the trial-averaged response at its amplitude,
for trial $j$ at amplitude $a$ in session $s$, where $x_{j}(t)$ is the onset-referenced trace and the sum runs over the $N = 18$ samples from 0 to 0.49\,s, the LTI fit window.
Unlike the evoked suppression (Eq.~\ref{eq:inhib_energy}), $e_{j}$ counts a dip that arrives early or late, or a rebound of the wrong size, as error.
Only nonzero amplitudes were analyzed (1516 trials in four sessions).
To pool amplitudes we scaled the error by its within-amplitude root mean square, $z_{j} = e_{j} / \mathrm{RMS}_{s,a}(e)$.
Each state measure ($[-1, 0)$\,s window) was converted to a within-session percentile, and trials were binned into quartiles of that percentile.
We summarize the pattern as the ratio of variability in the top to the bottom quartile, computed in each session and reported as the geometric mean of the four per-session ratios with their range.
With four sessions we attach no confidence intervals.
This analysis is descriptive: it sets up the pattern that the closed-loop experiments then test (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}), and the Results draw no inference from it.

For completeness, Table~\ref{tab:stat_fig2g} lists a supporting test: within each session, the ordinary least-squares slope of $z$ on state (standardized within session), and a one-sample $t$-test of the four slopes against zero (three degrees of freedom).
Two of the four sessions come from one mouse.
Pooled Spearman correlations are effect sizes only, without $p$-values, because trials within a session are not independent.

\emph{Stimulus-free window.} We repeated the quartile ratio and the pooled Spearman correlation on a matched quantity that contains no stimulus: Eq.~\eqref{eq:l2_error} over the 18 samples from $-1.51$ to $-1.03$\,s, referenced to the first sample of that window and compared with that window's mean trace at the same amplitude, then scaled in the same way.
This window lies before the state window, and the response window does not overlap it.
A state that changes the spread of this control as much as that of the response acts on the amplitude of ongoing activity rather than on the response to the stimulus.

Fig.~\ref{fig:state_quartile} divides each session's response variability by its stimulus-free variability in every quartile, a ratio that stays flat for such a state, and shows the single-trial errors.
It also shows single trials sorted by state at one amplitude per session (each session's second-highest), in raw $\Delta F/F$.

Its supporting test (Table~\ref{tab:stat_fig2g}) compares the top quartile of this ratio with the mean of the other three (one-sample $t$-test on the four per-session log ratios, three degrees of freedom).
Contralateral prediction and disturbance rejection
On spontaneous, no-laser frames we fitted a ridge-regularized linear predictor from contralateral pixels to the ipsilateral readout.
Predictors were about 500 pixels on a uniform lattice over the contralateral cortex, each z-scored on the training data.
Spontaneous frames were split in time, the first two thirds for training and the last third for testing, and we report the held-out $R^{2}$.

The ridge penalty was chosen without stimulation trials: it was the smallest penalty at which the predictor's spurious deflection on 200 laser-free catch windows (trial-shaped windows baselined like a real trial) stopped falling.
Held-out $R^2$ peaks near zero penalty and cannot set it.
On each stimulation trial we applied the fixed predictor to concurrent contralateral activity.

This gives the \emph{Global} component $G(t)$, an estimate of the ipsilateral activity expected with no controller input, and the \emph{Local} component $L(t) = A(t) - G(t)$, where $A(t)$ is the measured response.
We checked the decomposition by reconstructing $A$ as $G$ plus the leave-one-trial-out average local response, and report the cross-validated $R^{2}$ of that reconstruction over 0--3\,s.
We quantified rejection per trial as the energy ratio

where the numerator is the energy of the measured response about the reference $r = -5\%\,\Delta F/F$ and the denominator the energy of the disturbance $D$, the contralaterally predicted excursion referenced to its own no-laser baseline and leak-corrected.
Contralateral activity also changes during stimulation, so $G$ dips with the laser (in open loop by $6$--$42\%$ of the readout's dip over 0--3\,s, median $23\%$).
The leak correction subtracts, from each trial's $G$ referenced to the 1\,s before onset, the session's mean open-loop $G$ over the same window, so that $D$ keeps only the trial-to-trial excursion.
Both terms were evaluated over the steady-state window.

Referencing the disturbance to its own baseline rather than to the target keeps the fixed setpoint offset from being counted as disturbance, so $\mathrm{RR} < 1$ means the controlled response carries less energy than the disturbance it opposes.

We also computed $\mathrm{RR}$ on the open-loop trials of the same sessions, with the same window and leak correction, as a paired comparator in which any error in the scale of $D$ cancels between conditions.

For that comparison the numerator was split into the standing offset $(\bar{A}-r)^{2}$ and the fluctuation $\mathrm{var}(A)$, which separates a response sitting at the wrong level from one that fails to follow the disturbance.
Experimental Design and Statistical Analysis

\emph{Design.} Every closed-loop experiment is a within-session comparison: open- and closed-loop trials, with the same reference and feedforward term, were interleaved at random by the control software, so each session is its own control.

Sample sizes are 15 closed-loop sessions from 4 mice (2 male, 2 female; 1670 trials) for Figs.~\ref{fig:figure3} and~\ref{fig:figure4}, four impulse-response sessions from three mice for Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}, and three sinusoidal-tracking sessions from one mouse for Fig.~\ref{fig:figure5} (Table~\ref{tab:cohort}).
The unit of replication for every between-condition claim is the session, and we state $n$ with its unit for every test.
No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size.
We recorded as many sessions per animal as window clarity and opsin expression allowed.
Analyses were not blinded to condition.
All analyses were automated and applied identically to every condition.
\emph{Software and inference.} Analyses were performed in MATLAB R2025b.

The statistics of Figs.~\ref{fig:figure3} and~\ref{fig:figure4}D were reproduced independently in Python (SciPy 1.18) from the stored session data; per-trial RMSE agreed to within $10^{-6}$ and every state slope to four decimals.
Except for the disturbance-rejection model of Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}G (below), each between-condition test is on one number per session.
The primary test is a two-sided one-sample $t$-test of these session values ($n_{\mathrm{sessions}} - 1$ degrees of freedom), with a $t$-based 95\% confidence interval.
The exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the same values is reported alongside, as a check that does not assume normality.

We did not base inference on a model with mouse as a random effect: with four mice, two of which contributed one session each, the mouse variance cannot be estimated, and in our data its degrees of freedom were close to one or below.
Instead we report the mouse level directly, as the number of mice whose mean agrees in sign with the overall effect, and as the largest $p$ obtained when each mouse is left out in turn.
Significance was taken at $\alpha = 0.05$, two-sided unless stated.

The Statistical tables give each effect as an estimate with its 95\% confidence interval, the test statistic with its degrees of freedom, the exact $p$-value and $n$ with its unit; the text gives the estimate and $p$.
Signed-rank tests are reported with their $V$ statistic for Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}G and by their exact $p$ elsewhere.
Every test is listed in full in the Statistical tables (Tables~\ref{tab:stat_counts}--\ref{tab:stat_fig4g}).
Fig.~\ref{fig:figure2}G is descriptive, with its supporting tests in Table~\ref{tab:stat_fig2g} (\nameref{sec:imp_state}).

Fig.~\ref{fig:figure5} rests on three sessions in one mouse, too few for a session-level test, so it is reported descriptively: the per-session direction of each effect and the pooled mean $\pm$ SD, with no significance tests.
The MPC replay (\nameref{sec:mpc}) is a simulation and is reported descriptively.
\emph{Closed versus open loop} (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure3}).

The session value is the ratio $r$ of the closed- to the open-loop value in a window (mean per-trial RMSE, or across-trial variance averaged over the window), so that $r < 1$ means closed loop was better, and we test $\log r$.
We report the geometric-mean ratio with its 95\% confidence interval and as a percentage reduction, $100\,(1 - r)$.
The primary window is the 3\,s of stimulation; its transient (0--1\,s) and steady-state (1--3\,s) parts are secondary.
The pre- and post-stimulation windows are controls, reported as the ratio and its confidence interval without a test, because a large $p$ there would not show that nothing changed.
The comparisons are pre-specified, one per metric and window, and are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

\emph{Best fixed input.} To separate the error that feedback removes from the error of the rough feedforward calibration, we compared closed loop with the best fixed input that each session's open-loop trials allow.

Under the trial-averaged model with an additive disturbance, an open-loop trial is $y_i(t) = b + h(t) + n_i(t)$, where $b$ is the trial-averaged level over the 1\,s before onset, $h$ the trial-averaged effect of the open-loop command and $n_i$ the trial's deviation from the trial average.
A command scaled by $c$ would give $b + c\,h(t) + n_i(t)$.
We chose $c$ to minimize the squared error to the reference over the 0--3\,s stimulation window on the same open-loop trials, which favors open loop, and capped it at the command limit.
We then compared closed-loop RMSE with the RMSE of these rescaled trials, as above.
Under this model the across-trial variance does not depend on $c$.

To ask whether feedback moved the command toward this input on its own, we correlated across sessions (Spearman) the best $c$ with the mean closed-loop command over 1--3\,s divided by the open-loop command.
\emph{State dependence} (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}D).

Within each session we standardized each state over that session's trials (open and closed loop together), so every slope is in $\%\,\Delta F/F$ of steady-state RMSE per within-session standard deviation of the state.
In each session we fitted ordinary least-squares lines of steady-state RMSE on the standardized state, separately for open- and closed-loop trials, and tested each slope across sessions as above.
This gives three properties of each state.
\emph{Predictability} is the open-loop slope: a positive slope means the uncontrolled disturbance grows with the state, so a fixed feedforward input anticipates the trial less well.
\emph{Regularizability} is the closed-loop slope: a slope indistinguishable from zero means the loop keeps the output regulated as the state changes, and a positive slope means it loses it.

\emph{Attenuation} is the closed- minus the open-loop slope of $\log \mathrm{RMSE}$, that is, the slope of $\log(\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{CL}}/\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{OL}})$ against state: how the fraction of open-loop error left by the loop, the empirical counterpart of the sensitivity function, changes with state.
We report it as the percentage change of that fraction per standard deviation.

The open-minus-closed-loop gap in mean RMSE, and the open- minus the closed-loop slope (gap trend), are listed in Table~\ref{tab:fig4_state_stats} but not interpreted: the gap is the result of Fig.~\ref{fig:figure3}, and the gap can widen through a rising open loop as much as through a holding closed loop.
The error decomposition of Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}C is descriptive and carries no test.
\emph{Disturbance rejection} (Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}G).

We tested $\log \mathrm{RR} \sim 1 + (1 \mid \mathrm{session})$, one-sided on the intercept, and report the geometric mean of $\mathrm{RR}$ with its 95\% confidence interval, corroborated by a one-sided signed-rank test on the per-session median ratios.

The mixed models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood and tested with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, capped at $n_{\mathrm{sessions}} - 1$ so that no test borrows trial-level degrees of freedom, with $t$-based confidence intervals on the same degrees of freedom.
Tests of $\mathrm{RR} < 1$, and of closed- below open-loop $\mathrm{RR}$, were one-sided because the hypothesis was directional and fixed before the analysis.
We report the mouse-nested model, $\log \mathrm{RR} \sim 1 + (1 \mid \mathrm{mouse}) + (1 \mid \mathrm{mouse}\!:\!\mathrm{session})$, alongside as the mouse-level result.
With three mice, one contributing a single session, its degrees of freedom are ${\approx}1.2$ and the mouse and session variances cannot be separated.
\emph{Multiple comparisons.} The state analysis of Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}D asks three questions of each of four states.
Each is a separate, pre-specified question, and the stars in Fig.~\ref{fig:figure4}D give its uncorrected $p$.
As a check, Table~\ref{tab:fig4_state_stats} also gives Holm-adjusted $p$-values within two families: predictability and regularizability (eight tests), and attenuation (four tests).
Each claim rests on one primary test; the Statistical tables also give the Wilcoxon test on the same session values.
In figures, *, ** and *** denote $p < 0.05$, $0.01$ and $0.001$, and n.s.\ denotes $p \ge 0.05$.
Each legend names the test, and the tables give exact $p$ values.
